target_audience: University STEM students or advanced high school calculus students

sections.title: The Perspective Shift: From Slope to Stretch
sections.content: Introduce the idea that while derivatives are often seen as the 'slope of a tangent line' on a graph, they can also be viewed as a 'local scaling factor' between two number lines. This section transitions the viewer from the static x-y coordinate plane to a dynamic mapping perspective.
sections.example: Imagine two parallel horizontal number lines: an Input Line (x) and an Output Line (y). Instead of a curve, we draw 'mapping arrows' connecting points on x to points on y.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Linear Mapping
sections.content: Before tackling curves, understand how a linear function transforms space. If f(x) = 2x, every interval on the input line is stretched by a factor of 2 on the output line. This 'stretching constant' is the simplest form of a derivative.
sections.example: A 'Rubber Band' is stretched between two pegs on the input line. When mapped to the output line via f(x)=2x, the band becomes exactly twice as long, regardless of where it starts.

sections.title: The Local Scaling Factor
sections.content: For non-linear functions, the stretching isn't uniform. Introduce the derivative f'(x) as the specific 'zoom factor' at a single point. If you nudge 'x' by a tiny amount (dx), the output 'y' moves by dy. The derivative is the ratio: how much the space is being locally expanded or compressed.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Magnifying Glass' moving along the input line. Inside the glass, the mapping looks linear. The 'Magnification Power' printed on the glass is the value of the derivative at that spot.

sections.title: Application: The Square-Bot’s Journey
sections.content: Apply the transformational view to f(x) = x². Show that as we move further from the origin, the mapping arrows spread out significantly, meaning the 'stretching factor' (the derivative) is increasing.
sections.example: A character named 'Square-Bot' walks from x=1 to x=3. At x=1, a tiny step results in a step of size 2 (f'(1)=2). At x=3, the same tiny step on the input line causes a massive leap of size 6 on the output line (f'(3)=6). The space is being 'stretched' more aggressively as Square-Bot moves right.

sections.title: The Chain Rule: Compounding Stretches
sections.content: Demonstrate why this view makes the Chain Rule intuitive. If one function stretches space by 2 and the next stretches it by 3, the total stretch is the product (2 * 3 = 6).
sections.example: Two machines in a factory: Machine A stretches a piece of dough by f'(x), and Machine B stretches it again by g'(f(x)). The total change in length is the product of the two scaling factors.

sections.title: Summary and Intuition
sections.content: Summarize that f'(x) > 1 means expansion, 0 < f'(x) < 1 means compression, and f'(x) < 0 means the space is being flipped (mirrored) and stretched.
sections.example: A summary graphic showing a 'Density Map': where the derivative is high, input points are 'scattered' wide; where the derivative is low, input points are 'crushed' together.
